evaluated.name: Value Gated by Going-Concern Flags
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), ADD(INDICATOR(re, 0), INDICATOR(SUB(act, lct), 0)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value premium is conditional: it accrues to cheap firms with positive retained earnings and positive working capital, while cheap firms failing both going-concern screens have valuations that reflect genuine default risk and earn no premium.
evaluated.reasoning: The indicator sum acts as a 0/1/2 multiplier that switches the value exposure off for firms with a deficit in accumulated earnings and a liquidity shortfall, so extreme cheapness among distressed firms is collapsed to the bottom of the cross-section. This is an explicitly conditional interaction rather than an additive blend of two effects. Winsorizing book-to-market prevents a handful of near-zero-market-cap firms from dominating the long leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheapness Times Deleveraging
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What separates value opportunities from traps is the direction of the distress state: cheap firms actively reducing their liability burden are recovering and repricing upward, while equally cheap firms whose leverage is rising are sliding toward distress.
evaluated.reasoning: The cheapness rank sets the magnitude of the bet and the year-over-year change in the liabilities-to-assets ratio sets its direction, so the signal goes long cheap deleveraging firms and short cheap re-levering firms. This uses a change-in-distress state rather than a level screen, capturing information that static leverage filters miss. Winsorizing the leverage change limits distortion from restructurings and large acquisitions.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Weakest-Link Value Solvency Score
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Compensated value requires cheapness and solvency jointly, so the firm's score should be its worst dimension: a deeply cheap firm with no accumulated earnings and no cash relative to debt is a distress trap, not a value opportunity, and must not be rescued by its cheapness rank.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the additive SUMRANK blend with MIN of the two ranked dimensions makes the score non-compensatory, so a firm ranks high only if it is simultaneously in the cheap tail and the solvent tail — the claim the earlier version could not support. Both arguments are rescaled to a common [0,1] rank metric before the MIN so neither dimension mechanically dominates the binding constraint. The short leg is now firms that are weak on at least one dimension, which is precisely the expensive-or-distressed population the economic story targets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap Non-Taxpayer
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(txt, at), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash taxes are an independently verified signature of real, sustained earnings; a cheap firm that has paid essentially no tax over three years is generating no taxable income and its discount reflects genuine economic deterioration rather than sentiment.
evaluated.reasoning: Tax expense is harder to manage than accrual earnings, so persistent non-payment identifies distressed cheapness that accounting-based profitability screens can miss, giving a distinct channel from leverage, liquidity, and margins. The three-year moving average enforces persistence rather than a one-off loss year, matching the "severe distress" wording of the economic story. Ranking both components keeps the trap cell in the top of the score without letting tax outliers dominate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap at Own Liquidity Trough
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(wcap, at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress is a firm-relative state: a cheap stock whose working-capital-to-assets ratio sits at the bottom of its own five-year history is deteriorating toward a funding constraint, whereas a cheap stock at a normal position in its own liquidity history is simply out of favor.
evaluated.reasoning: Using position-in-own-history rather than a cross-sectional level removes the industry and business-model component of working capital, so the distress reading is about change of state rather than static balance-sheet style. This tests whether the trap effect is driven by deterioration or by static weakness, a question the level-based signals in this batch cannot answer. Five annual observations are enough for a stable TS_RANK while keeping coverage acceptable for established firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap With Cash-Flow Insolvency
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The trap is not leverage per se but the inability of internally generated cash to service the total liability stack; a cheap firm whose operating cash flow is small or negative relative to total liabilities is pricing in an eventual restructuring, and such firms earn low subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the product with MIN removes the sign ambiguity the critic identified: a cheap firm with healthy cash-flow coverage now scores low, so the top of the distribution is populated only by the joint cheap-and-cash-insolvent cell rather than by cheap firms generally. The distress channel is Beaver's cash-flow-to-total-liabilities coverage, which is absent from the archive's leverage, retained-earnings, and working-capital screens, so this tests a funding-capacity mechanism rather than a stock-of-solvency mechanism. Both inputs are near-universally reported, keeping coverage comparable to prior signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidation-Backed Cheapness
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness is safe when the entire liability stack can be extinguished out of current assets alone; the residual liquid value per dollar of market capitalization measures cheapness that survives full creditor satisfaction, whereas cheapness resting on illiquid book assets behind heavy claims is a distress discount.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the RANK(B/M)×RANK(distress) template entirely: creditor claims are subtracted inside the valuation numerator rather than applied as a separate screen, so leverage and asset liquidity change what counts as book value instead of gating it. It differs from the archive's act−lct going-concern flag because total liabilities, not just current liabilities, are netted, making the measure a solvency-adjusted valuation rather than a working-capital indicator. Winsorizing controls the micro-cap tail where market capitalization is tiny relative to net liquid assets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Contributed Rather Than Earned Cheapness
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(re, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two firms with identical book-to-market differ fundamentally in whether their book equity was earned or contributed: a firm whose book value consists of paid-in capital offset by accumulated deficits has financed itself by dilution and burned the proceeds, so its apparent cheapness reflects a chronic loss-financing life cycle rather than mispriced earning power.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the flagged sales-versus-profit version, this difference does not collapse into a margin — it isolates contributed capital per dollar of price, a life-cycle and financing-distress construct orthogonal to the profitability factor. Both ranks share the same price denominator by design, so the value dimension nets out and what remains is purely the earned-versus-contributed composition of the book value that makes the firm look cheap. Retained earnings enter as a level relative to price rather than as a solvency flag, distinguishing it from the archive's INDICATOR(re, 0) gate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unlevered Versus Levered Cheapness Gap
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(ADD(ceq, lt), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt))), RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity-level cheapness has two sources — genuinely discounted operating assets and pure financial leverage magnifying a modest asset discount — and only the first is compensated; firms whose asset base is cheap on an unlevered basis without extreme equity-level cheapness are the healthy value cases, while firms cheap only after leverage magnification are distress traps.
evaluated.reasoning: This decomposes the value signal rather than conditioning it, so it does not reduce to industry-neutral book-to-market for the bulk of the cross-section the way the SIGN(re) gate did — the score is defined and differentiated for every firm with reported liabilities. Adding total liabilities to both numerator and denominator converts equity book-to-market into an asset-level market-to-book, and the rank difference measures exactly how much of the observed equity cheapness is leverage-manufactured. Because the two components carry similar HML exposure, the spread should be substantially factor-neutral, targeting alpha rather than a repackaged value premium.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Working-Capital Backed Cheapness
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: If the liquidation-backing effect is about near-term funding safety rather than full solvency, then netting only current liabilities from current assets should capture most of it; if long-term creditor claims are what separate healthy from distressed cheapness, this variant should be markedly weaker.
evaluated.reasoning: This is deliberately a one-input contrast with the archive winner: it removes long-term liabilities from the netting so that the difference in results identifies whether the alpha comes from short-horizon liquidity or from total creditor overhang. That distinction matters economically because the two imply different risks — refinancing pressure versus permanent capital impairment — and it cannot be inferred from the existing evaluations. Winsorization matches the archive construction so the comparison is not confounded by scaling.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidation Backing With Cash Generation
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(oancf, lct)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net liquid asset backing is a stock of safety that a cash-burning firm consumes; cheapness is genuinely healthy only when the liquid cushion is not being eroded by operating outflows relative to current obligations.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN structure makes the score high only when both the liquidation cushion and the operating cash coverage of current liabilities are strong, so it tests whether adding a flow condition to the winning stock condition sharpens the FF5 alpha or merely shrinks the eligible universe. Because a static balance-sheet cushion says nothing about its rate of depletion, this is the most economically natural refinement of the archive's best result rather than a rescaling of it. If the alpha rises with only mild coverage loss, the mechanism is confirmed as solvency plus sustainability; if not, the effect is purely a stock-of-liquidity phenomenon.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Resources Net of Current Claims to Price
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(che, oancf), lct), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The safest form of cheapness is one where cash on hand plus a year of operating cash flow already exceeds all current obligations, so the equity price is backed by resources that cannot be impaired by inventory or receivable write-downs.
evaluated.reasoning: Together with Signals 1 and 2 this triangulates the composition of the liquidation-backing effect — total current assets, current assets net of current liabilities, and now the strictly verifiable cash-plus-cash-flow subset — so the batch identifies which assets the market fails to price rather than merely re-testing one construct. Including the operating cash flow term makes the measure a resource-versus-claims comparison over the coming year rather than a static snapshot. The market-cap denominator is strictly positive, avoiding the sign-flip pathology that afflicted enterprise-value deflators.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Absolute Liquidation Discount to Firm Size
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), at), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The compensated form of cheapness is an absolute dollar discount of market capitalization below net liquid asset value, sized relative to the firm's asset base rather than relative to its own depressed price, so that the signal measures the margin of safety rather than the smallness of the price.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a monotone transform of the archived winner: the discount enters as a difference rather than a quotient and is deflated by total assets instead of market capitalization, so the quantile portfolios and their size composition genuinely change. That distinction is the substantive test the critic asked for — if the archived alpha is really a micro-cap price-scaling artifact it should weaken here, whereas if it is a true asset-value discount it should survive with a better behaved regressor and a stronger FMB slope. Winsorization handles the residual tail without altering the ordering of the bulk of firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheapness Backed by Liquid Book Quality
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ceq)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two firms with the same book-to-market differ in whether their book equity is composed of liquid assets net of all claims or of fixed and intangible assets standing behind creditors; only cheapness whose book value is liquid-backed is compensated, because that collateral survives a downturn.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that a dollar complement collapses to non-current-assets-to-price, a known positively priced quantity with the wrong sign, so the revision changes the construct to a *composition* ratio — net liquid assets as a fraction of book equity — which is a quality-of-book measure, not an assets-to-price measure. The MIN form makes the score high only when the firm is both cheap and liquid-backed, so it directly separates the two kinds of cheap firms the theme is about rather than re-testing the value premium. It also asks a question the archive cannot answer: whether the liquidation effect works through book quality conditional on cheapness or only through the absolute price discount.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Earnings Yield Pledged to Creditors
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high cash-earnings yield is a value signal only when shareholders can actually keep the cash; in heavily levered firms the same operating earnings are effectively pledged to creditors, so the apparently cheap multiple compensates for a claim that equity holders do not own.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing dividends with EBITDA removes the zero-payout tie block the critic identified — both legs are now continuously distributed across essentially the whole universe, so the top region is a clean high-yield, high-leverage cell and the bottom region is differentiated rather than dominated by non-payers. The economic content is preserved and arguably sharper: it contrasts cash generation that accrues to equity with cash generation that services debt, which is exactly the healthy-versus-trap distinction. It also complements the batch's liquidation-backing signals by testing the flow side of the same creditor-priority mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dual-Deflated Liquid Claim Coverage
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ceq))
evaluated.hypothesis: Net liquid assets matter both relative to what the market is paying and relative to the accounting book value they are supposed to support; combining the two views identifies firms that are cheap *and* whose book equity is genuinely liquid, rather than firms that are merely tiny in market value.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive shows the price-deflated version carries the alpha (t=4.48) while the book-deflated composition version carries the cross-sectional slope (t=4.02), so this directly tests whether the two sources of evidence are additive or substitutes. SUMRANK reorders the extreme tail — a firm with a huge discount but a book value composed of illiquid assets no longer dominates — which is a substantive change in portfolio composition, not a rescaling. If both metrics improve jointly, the combined construct becomes the consolidation candidate for later generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidation Discount With Stable Cushion
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A liquid cushion trading at a discount is compensated only if it is not being consumed; firms whose net-liquid-assets-to-assets ratio fell over the past year are financing losses out of the very cushion that makes them look cheap.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's cash-generation filter delivered a good alpha (4.5%) and slope (2.88) but cut coverage from 0.122 to 0.079 because operating cash flow is sparsely reported early in the sample; measuring depletion from the balance sheet itself preserves coverage while testing the same stock-versus-flow economics. Comparing this signal's results with the oancf version isolates whether the sustainability condition needs a genuine cash-flow statement or can be inferred from the change in the cushion. The MIN keeps the top region restricted to firms that are both deeply discounted and not depleting.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquid Cushion per Dollar of Total Claims
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Scaling the liquid cushion by the total market value of all claims — equity plus creditor claims — measures how much of the entire capital structure is already covered by liquid assets, distinguishing genuinely over-collateralized firms from small-equity firms whose discount is an artifact of a collapsed share price sitting on top of heavy debt.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's asset-deflated version destroyed the alpha while raising the slope, so the denominator is doing the economic work and deserves one more disciplined test: total claims keeps price in the denominator (preserving the market-relative discount) but adds liabilities, damping the extreme tail generated by tiny market caps behind large debt. If alpha survives at a comparable level with a much stronger FMB slope, the leverage-inflated micro-cap tail was noise rather than signal; if alpha collapses like the asset-scaled version, the effect is specifically an equity-price phenomenon. Either outcome sharply narrows the search for later generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Fixed-Charge Burden Behind a Cheap Multiple
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, pi), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The wedge between EBITDA and pretax income is the firm's annual fixed charge — interest plus depreciation — so a cheap cash-earnings multiple sitting on top of a large fixed-charge load means the operating cash is committed before shareholders see it, making the cheapness a distress discount rather than an opportunity.
evaluated.reasoning: This measures debt-service and asset-consumption burden directly from the income statement rather than from balance-sheet leverage ratios, a channel absent from the entire archive, and it explains *why* the archive's leverage-pledged-earnings signal produced a −3.8% alpha. Because both legs are continuously distributed across nearly all firms, the top region is a clean high-yield, high-burden cell with no tie blocks. Its expected negative sign also gives the batch a short-side test to complement the four long-side liquidation constructs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Revenue Cheapness With Solvent Liquidity
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The healthy-cheap versus trap distinction should not be specific to balance-sheet valuation: a firm cheap on revenue is a compensated value case when its current assets already exceed all liabilities, and a distressed one when creditors have first claim on the entire asset base.
evaluated.reasoning: Every liquidation-family result in the archive uses a balance-sheet numerator over price, so the effect could be a mechanical book-to-market artifact; substituting a revenue-based valuation anchor tests whether liquid solvency conditions the value premium generally or only its book-based form. Deflating the cushion by assets here is deliberate — the price dimension already enters through the sales multiple, so the two legs stay economically independent. Sales are reported nearly universally, so coverage should match the archive's best signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Worst-Case Liquid Cushion to Price
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_MIN(SUB(act, lt), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The collateral that protects a cheap stock is not the cushion reported at one convenient date but the minimum net liquid position the firm has actually sustained over recent years; measuring the discount against that demonstrated floor separates durably over-collateralized firms from those whose current-year cushion was manufactured by an asset sale, a debt drawdown, or a working-capital build.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces smoothing with a conservative floor: only the numerator uses history, so the denominator remains the current market capitalization and the stale-price contamination the critic identified is eliminated entirely. It is economically distinct from the archive winner because it reorders firms by the reliability of their creditor-adjusted liquid backing rather than by its latest level, which is exactly the healthy-versus-illusory-cheapness distinction and should stabilize portfolio composition and raise ls_talpha. The three-year window is short enough to keep coverage close to the archive's 0.12 while still requiring the cushion to have survived a full reporting cycle.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Worst-Case Cushion With Profitable Operations
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(TS_MIN(SUB(act, lt), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(pi, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A deep discount to a durable liquid cushion is compensated mispricing when the operating business is still profitable, and a rational forecast of cash burn when it is not; the profitable subset of deeply discounted firms should carry the entire abnormal return.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's one attempt to add a viability condition used operating cash flow and cut coverage from 0.122 to 0.079 while still delivering 4.5% alpha with a 2.88 slope; pretax income is reported far earlier and more broadly, so this tests the same economics without the sample truncation that muddied the comparison. Conditioning the tail on profitability should also make the extreme decile less junk-like, which is precisely the fix needed to raise the FMB slope while retaining the 6.4% alpha of the worst-case cushion. If both metrics rise together, this becomes the leading consolidation candidate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own-History Cheapness With Solvent Balance Sheet
evaluated.expression: MIN(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm trading at the cheapest valuation of its own five-year history is either being repriced for newly revealed distress or is temporarily out of favor; the solvency of its balance sheet decides which, so time-series cheapness conditioned on liquid solvency should isolate genuine mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: All archive valuation legs are cross-sectional, which conflates permanently cheap business models with firms that have actually de-rated; a within-firm valuation percentile removes that fixed effect and asks a different economic question. Combining it with an asset-scaled solvency leg keeps the price dimension in only one leg, so the two components remain economically independent. The five-year window costs some coverage, as it did for the archive's liquidity-trough signal (0.111), which is an acceptable price for testing a genuinely new valuation anchor.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unimpairable Cash Cushion to Price
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: In genuine distress, receivables are not collected and inventory sells at a fraction of carrying value, so only cash survives the state of the world that matters; a firm whose cash alone exceeds every liability and still trades at a discount holds collateral that cannot be impaired.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has repeatedly varied which *liabilities* are netted but never isolated which *assets* do the work with full coverage — the one cash-based attempt bundled in operating cash flow and lost a third of the sample. This changes the asset side while holding the liability definition and deflator fixed at the archive winner's, so a comparable alpha would show the effect is a pure cash-versus-claims phenomenon, while a much weaker one would prove that impairable working capital carries the mispricing. Both inputs are near-universally reported, so coverage should match the archive's 0.12 rather than the truncated 0.079.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Discount Without Dilution
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Management's financing behavior reveals which kind of cheap firm it is running: a firm sitting on a liquid cushion that keeps issuing shares is funding losses and diluting the very claim that looks cheap, whereas one whose share count is flat or shrinking is letting existing holders keep the discount.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a neutralization transform with a genuinely new arbiter — the corporate financing decision — which is observable, forward-looking, and absent from every archive signal that has relied purely on balance-sheet stocks and accounting flows. Share count changes are reported for essentially all firms, so unlike the operating-cash-flow filter this conditioning costs almost no coverage, and it should sharpen the deep-discount decile by removing serial issuers whose cushion per share is eroding. It also gives the batch a direct test of whether the cushion alpha is an ownership-dilution phenomenon rather than an asset-value phenomenon.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Volatile-Earnings Equity Stub
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When liabilities dwarf market capitalization the equity is effectively a deep out-of-the-money call on the firm's assets, and its value rises with fundamental volatility; investors overpay for this lottery-like optionality, so highly levered firms with unstable pretax earnings should earn low subsequent returns.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the market-versus-book leverage difference the critic showed collapses into asset-to-market, and instead pairs market-value leverage with a second moment of fundamentals — the combination that defines the "lottery-like trap" in the theme's own economic story and that no archive signal has tested. The two legs are economically independent (one is a capital-structure valuation ratio, the other a time-series risk measure), so the top region is a clean option-like stub cell rather than a restatement of the value premium. It supplies the batch's short-side test, where the archive's best trap alpha so far is only −3.8%.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Loss-Absorption Horizon at a Discount
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ABS(TS_MIN(pi, 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What makes a liquid cushion safe is not its size but how many years of the firm's own worst observed loss it can absorb; a deeply discounted firm whose cushion covers many such years cannot be forced to restructure, while one whose cushion covers less than a single bad year is priced for exactly that outcome.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than rank-averaging components already in the archive, this introduces a survival-horizon concept that is new to the search: the cushion is scaled by the firm's own historically worst pretax result, making the distress threshold firm-specific rather than cross-sectional. It should also repair the archive's central estimation problem, because the second leg demotes the many deeply discounted micro-caps whose cushion is small relative to their loss history — precisely the lumpy tail that has kept FMB slopes near zero while alphas were large. The five-year pretax history is the only coverage cost, comparable to the archive's other temporal signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Runway Against Operating Cost Base
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), SUB(revt, pi))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Survival is determined by how long the liquid cushion could fund the firm's actual cost base, so scaling net liquid assets by annual operating costs gives a runway in years that separates a cheap firm with a decade of self-funding from one with a single quarter.
evaluated.reasoning: The loss-absorption idea worked but required five years of pretax history and used a single worst-year outlier as the denominator; revenue minus pretax income is the firm's total annual cost base, is available contemporaneously for essentially every firm, and is a smoother, more continuous measure of burn capacity. Because the second leg is again cushion-based, the deep-discount tail should survive intersection, while the continuity of the runway variable should improve the cross-sectional slope that the outlier-based version could not deliver. Comparing it with Signal 1 identifies whether survival capacity is better measured against historical loss extremes or ongoing cost scale.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Two-Sided Cushion and Earnings Stability Score
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The theme has two distinct payoffs — asset-backed cheapness earns a premium and option-like unstable-earnings equity loses — so a score that is high for over-collateralized firms with stable fundamentals and low for liability-heavy firms with volatile fundamentals should capture both sides in one spread.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive documents the long side (cushion discount, +6%) and the short side (volatile-earnings stub, −4.4% with t=−3.27) as separate signals; rank-averaging them keeps the deep-discount firms at the top rather than filtering them out, while the volatility leg populates the bottom with genuine lottery-like stubs instead of merely levered firms. Because SUMRANK is additive, the middle of the distribution becomes monotone in two economically independent channels, which is the structural fix for the near-zero FMB slopes that pure tail signals produce. The five-year volatility window costs modest coverage, as the stub signal's 0.130 shows.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discounted Cushion Without Forced-Restructuring Risk
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), act))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only contractual debt can force a restructuring that wipes out equity; a firm trading below its net liquid asset value with little interest-bearing debt relative to those liquid assets cannot be pushed into bankruptcy, so its discount must close through operations, asset sales, or payouts.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive nets total liabilities but never distinguishes enforceable debt from trade and accrued claims that carry no default trigger, and this leg is cushion-correlated (debt is a component of the liabilities already netted) so it should refine the alpha decile rather than replace it. Economically it converts the signal from "cheap relative to assets" to "cheap relative to assets and immune to forced liquidation", which is the sharpest version of the healthy-cheap side of the theme. Coverage is unaffected because debt items are near-universally reported.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Levered Diluter Death Spiral
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(GROWTH(csho, 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose liabilities dwarf its market value and which is simultaneously issuing shares is funding creditor obligations by diluting equity holders at depressed prices, a self-reinforcing transfer from shareholders to creditors that predicts continued underperformance.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates the financing behavior that turns market-value leverage into realized equity loss, a mechanism the archive has approached only from the asset side and never tested on the short side. Both legs are continuously distributed with no tie blocks among the levered universe, and the pairing is economically tight: neither high market leverage alone nor issuance alone identifies the transfer, but their intersection does. A reliable negative alpha here would give the search a genuine short-leg mechanism to pair with the cushion long leg in the final consolidation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Productive Cushion at a Discount
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(revt, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms trading below net liquid asset value split into two economically opposite groups — working businesses whose inventory and receivables are turning over to generate sales, and dormant shells whose current assets sit idle while overhead consumes them — and only the productive group's discount closes.
evaluated.reasoning: This introduces asset productivity, a channel the archive has never tested, in place of recombining two collinear cushion constructs: revenue per dollar of current assets says whether the collateral is a live operating base or a stagnant pile, which is the sharpest available distinction between compensated cheapness and a slow-burning trap. Because the second leg shares the current-asset base with the first, it should refine the deep-discount decile rather than displace it — the failure mode the no-dilution intersection exposed. Both inputs are universally reported, so coverage should hold near the archive's 0.12.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discount Plus Per-Share Cushion Accretion
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), GROWTH(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), csho), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: What protects the holder of a cheap asset-backed equity is not the share count and not the total cushion separately, but whether net liquid assets *per share* are rising; a firm accreting liquid value per share is compounding the discount in the owner's favor, while one whose per-share cushion is shrinking is either burning assets or issuing stock against them.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not the earlier operator swap: the second leg is a new quantity that fuses the asset-accumulation and dilution channels the archive tested separately, resolving why the no-dilution filter helped the cross-sectional slope but destroyed the tail — issuance only matters when it outpaces cushion growth. The additive combination keeps deeply discounted firms at the top of the score while the accretion leg, which is continuous and roughly symmetric, orders the middle of the distribution and should lift the FMB slope. Coverage costs only one year of history, keeping the sample close to the archive's best signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap Book Value in Asset-Heavy Firms
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), revt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: If the effect is really about balance-sheet dominance rather than about the specific net-net threshold, then ordinary book-to-market conditioned on a large liquid cushion per dollar of revenue should reproduce it; if instead the price-below-liquid-assets condition is essential, this variant will be much weaker.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the decisive ablation the archive still lacks: every strong result has used net liquid assets in the numerator over price, so we cannot yet tell whether the alpha requires that specific comparison or only requires cheapness plus an operations-light liquid balance sheet. Book-to-market has repeatedly produced strong FMB slopes (3.5–4.0) with weak or negative alphas in this archive, so pairing it with the newly identified conditioner tests directly whether that conditioner is what converts a factor-explained value tilt into abnormal return. Coverage matches the archive's best signals since all inputs are standard.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discount With Uninflated Working Capital
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(SUB(GROWTH(act, 1), GROWTH(revt, 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A liquid cushion is only worth its carrying value if it is turning over; when current assets grow far faster than sales, the balance sheet is accumulating unsellable inventory and uncollectible receivables, so the apparent liquidation floor is overstated and the cheapness is a genuine distress signal.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive test of cushion quality has varied which claims are netted or how large the cushion is; none has questioned whether the reported current assets are realizable, which is exactly the accounting failure that turns a net-net into a trap. The leg is a difference of two growth rates, so it is continuously distributed and roughly symmetric — the property that lifted the FMB slope in the two-sided score — while remaining economically tied to the cushion rather than orthogonal to it. This is the batch's most direct attempt to raise the cross-sectional slope without truncating the alpha-bearing tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt-Free Cash Earnings Yield
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), act))))
evaluated.hypothesis: On the earnings side of valuation, cheapness is compensated when no enforceable debt stands between the operating cash flow and the shareholder; a high cash-earnings yield with interest-bearing debt small relative to liquid assets is the going-concern analogue of a net-net.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has tested the earnings channel almost exclusively on the trap side — high yield with high leverage or high fixed charges, both around −4% alpha — so the symmetric positive case has never been evaluated, leaving the theme's central claim only half tested. Scaling debt by current assets rather than total assets measures whether the enforceable claims could be extinguished immediately, which is the distress-relevant comparison and mirrors the construct that scored best in generation 5 (5.6% alpha, t=4.11). Both legs are broadly reported, so coverage should stay near 0.14.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discount With Non-Expanding Claims
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(lt, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A liquid cushion priced at a discount is safe only if creditors are not expanding their claim on it; rising total liabilities mean the firm is funding operations by borrowing against the very assets that constitute the margin of safety.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has conditioned the cushion on its own change and on share issuance but never on the growth of the claims that are netted out of it, even though liability expansion is the mechanism by which a net-net silently becomes a levered shell. The leg is cushion-related through lt, so it should refine rather than displace the top decile — the distinction generation 4 established between correlated and orthogonal conditioners. It also gives a clean contrast with Signal 3: asset-side inflation versus liability-side expansion as competing explanations for why a cushion fails to protect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Negative Implied Price of Operations
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(act, lt)), revt)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Market capitalization decomposes into the net liquid cushion plus whatever the market is paying for the operating business; when that residual stub price is deeply negative relative to the revenue the business actually produces, investors are being handed the operations for free because they extrapolate current operating disappointment.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than re-scaling the cushion by another operating denominator — the collinearity the critic identified — this construct isolates the *residual* the archive has never measured: price minus cushion, which is the market's standalone valuation of the going concern, benchmarked against the revenue that concern generates. It states the theme's core question directly, because a negative stub price means the valuation reflects operating distress while the distress-relevant collateral is intact and unpriced. Revenue is strictly positive for the operating universe, so the deflator does not sign-flip, and the measure is continuous across the whole cross-section rather than being a tail indicator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Claims Outgrowing the Business Behind Them
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUB(GROWTH(lt, 1), GROWTH(revt, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A levered firm becomes a trap when its creditor claims expand faster than the revenue base that must service them; the equity of such a firm is a shrinking residual on a widening obligation, and its low valuation is a forecast rather than a discount.
evaluated.reasoning: The second leg is a new quantity for this archive — the divergence between liability growth and revenue growth — rather than a merger of the previously tested volatility and issuance gates, and it captures deterioration in debt-servicing capacity that no static leverage ratio or second-moment measure can express. Pairing it with market-value leverage is what makes the claim cross-theme: the same liability expansion is benign for a firm whose equity is richly valued and lethal for one whose market value is already a stub. Both legs are continuously distributed with no tie blocks, and only one year of history is required, so coverage should remain near 0.13.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Backing Minus Claim Escalation
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(SUB(GROWTH(lt, 1), GROWTH(revt, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The two ends of this theme are distinct populations: over-collateralized cheap firms earn a premium, and firms whose creditor claims are growing faster than the revenue that must service them underperform, so a single score should rank the first group at the top and the second at the bottom.
evaluated.reasoning: The claim-escalation leg produced the archive's cleanest short-side result (−4.1% alpha, t=−3.54) but, used as a MIN gate, growth legs have consistently destroyed the long tail; combining additively lets each leg populate its own extreme without the intersection truncating either. This is the only construction in the archive that puts a genuinely different economic population in each leg rather than filtering one population twice. If it delivers a mid-single-digit alpha with a materially positive slope, it resolves the archive's central tension by construction rather than by transformation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Chronic Net-Net Status Count
evaluated.expression: TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 0), 5)
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of market capitalization below net liquid asset value can be a stale price or a transient dislocation, but a firm that has satisfied this condition in most of the last five years is persistently and knowably over-collateralized, and the market's continued refusal to price the collateral is the mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the deflator recombination with a genuinely different construction — a discrete count of how many annual observations satisfied the balance-sheet-versus-price condition, rather than another continuous ratio whose slope the archive has repeatedly shown to be near zero. A five-level integer regressor is exactly the kind of well-conditioned variable that can produce a meaningful Fama-MacBeth slope, and it selects the top portfolio on persistence rather than on the magnitude of a skewed ratio, so the portfolios differ substantively from every archive signal. The trade-off is a large tie block at zero, which the coverage and Sharpe diagnostics will reveal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own-History Extreme Asset Discount
evaluated.expression: TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5)
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms differ permanently in how much liquid collateral their business model carries, so what identifies mispricing is not the level of the asset discount but whether a firm now sits at the widest discount of its own recent history — the point at which the market has repriced the equity without any corresponding change in the collateral.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the flagged price-drawdown leg, the valuation anchor here is not the price path but the price relative to a contemporaneous balance-sheet quantity, so it is not a restatement of nearness-to-high or long-horizon reversal; a firm can reach its own extreme through a falling price or a growing cushion, and both are informative about the same wedge. Within-firm ranking removes the permanent industry and business-model component that makes the cross-sectional level so lumpy and tail-concentrated, which is the archive's diagnosed cause of near-zero slopes. Coverage should land near 0.11, consistent with other five-year constructs in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Levered Firm Liquidating Its Current Assets
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(act, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm whose liabilities already dwarf its market value is shrinking its current assets, it is meeting obligations by consuming inventory and collecting receivables without replacing them — an orderly self-liquidation in which the equity holder is last in line and receives nothing.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the contested price-path leg entirely and pairs market-value leverage with a purely accounting measure of balance-sheet contraction, a channel the archive has never tested on the short side and one that is economically distinct from liability growth, share issuance, and earnings volatility. The two legs share no variable, so the top region isolates precisely the levered-and-contracting cell the hypothesis names, and the interpretation does not depend on the composition of the bottom region. Both inputs are universally reported, so coverage should hold near 0.13 with only one year of history required.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Claims Value per Dollar of Liquid Assets
evaluated.expression: NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Every claim on a firm — equity at market value and liabilities at face value — is ultimately a claim on its assets, so the price the market places on each dollar of liquid current assets is the cleanest statement of asset-backed cheapness; paying little for each such dollar is compensated, paying much is not.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a monotone transform of the total-claims cushion signal: that measure is (act−lt)/(ME+lt), a function of two independent ratios, whereas this is (ME+lt)/act, which orders firms differently whenever leverage and market valuation move apart. Because the denominator is gross current assets, the quantity is strictly positive and bounded away from the explosive skew that has kept the archive's FMB slopes near zero, giving a plausible path to joint strength rather than tail-only alpha. It also treats creditors and shareholders symmetrically, which is the correct economics when asking what the market pays for liquid collateral.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap Liquid Assets With Covered Claims
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act)), RATIO(pi, lt))
evaluated.hypothesis: Healthy cheapness combines a low price per dollar of liquid assets with pretax earnings large enough to service the outstanding claims; the trap is the opposite corner, where claims are expensive relative to liquid assets and earnings cannot cover them.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not an operator swap on an existing pair: both legs are new to the archive — the price paid per dollar of liquid assets and pretax income scaled by total claims rather than by assets, which measures debt-service capacity rather than profitability. Because the two legs use different accounting anchors and neither is a monotone function of the other, the additive score populates its extremes with economically different firms, giving genuinely new portfolio evidence rather than a smoothed version of a tested spread. Both components are continuously distributed across essentially the whole universe, which is the property most likely to convert the archive's tail-only alpha into a signal with a coherent cross-sectional slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Discount With Cash-Heavy Collateral
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(che, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two firms with identical net liquid cushions differ in how much of that cushion is cash rather than inventory and receivables; the cash-heavy one can actually deliver the collateral to shareholders, while the inventory-heavy one holds assets whose realizable value falls precisely when the firm needs it.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has tested cash *instead of* working capital — the cash-only cushion delivered a weaker 3.9% alpha with a negative Sharpe — but never cash as a *composition* condition on the full cushion, which is a different economic claim about realizability rather than about which assets to count. The gate is a ratio of components of the same current-asset base, so it should refine the deep-discount decile rather than replace it with an orthogonal population. Interpreted alongside Signal 4, it separates the two ways a cushion can fail: unrealizable assets versus inflexible creditors.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Discount With Flexible Creditors
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for a discounted firm is not how large its liabilities are but who holds them: trade payables and accruals can be renegotiated or stretched in a downturn, whereas bondholders and banks can accelerate, so a cushion standing behind mostly non-financial claims is far safer at the same leverage.
evaluated.reasoning: Every leverage-related conditioner in the archive has measured the *magnitude* of claims — debt over assets, debt over current assets, liability growth — and none has measured their *composition*, even though creditor type determines whether distress becomes a forced event. Scaling debt by total liabilities rather than by an asset base makes this a pure mix variable, uncorrelated with firm size and only mildly correlated with the leverage levels already tested. Contrasting its result with Signal 2, which uses the same debt items scaled by current assets, identifies whether coverage or creditor identity is the operative mechanism.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Depth Plus Cheap Liquid Assets
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The depth of the net-of-claims discount and the price paid per gross dollar of liquid assets are two distinct statements about the same balance sheet — the first is extreme and tail-concentrated, the second smooth and pervasive — and a firm ranked highly on both is cheap in a way that neither measure alone establishes.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the last disciplined attempt to close the archive's central gap: the first leg carries essentially all of the documented alpha (5.9%, t=4.48) but a slope of 0.48, while the second leg carries a 4.17 slope and Sharpe 0.411 with almost no alpha, and the two are related but not monotone transforms of one another since one nets liabilities out of the numerator and the other adds them to it. Additive combination keeps deeply discounted firms near the top instead of intersecting them away, so a mid-to-high single-digit alpha with a slope above 2 is a realistic outcome rather than a smoothing artifact. If it succeeds it becomes the final recommended signal; if it fails, the evidence will have shown the alpha and the slope to be genuinely irreconcilable in this family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Stress-Tested Cushion to Price
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), ABS(TS_MIN(DELTA(SUB(act, lt), 1), 5))), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The collateral that should support a cheap equity is not today's net liquid position but what would remain after a repeat of the worst single-year erosion the firm has actually experienced; a discount to that stress-tested residual is a discount to collateral the firm has demonstrated it can retain under duress.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a lookback-window tweak: the history is used to estimate a firm-specific shock magnitude — the largest annual decline in net current assets — which is then subtracted from the current cushion, producing a value-at-risk style collateral measure that no archive signal computes. It targets the failure mode the whole family faces, namely cushions that evaporate between reporting dates, and because it remains a single continuous ratio it cannot truncate the alpha-bearing decile the way conditioning gates repeatedly have. Firms with volatile working capital are demoted even when their current cushion looks large, so the portfolio composition differs materially from the archived three-year-minimum version.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Either-Form Collateral Discount
evaluated.expression: MAX(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms hold unpriced collateral in different forms — some as working capital in excess of all claims, others as cash in excess of interest-bearing debt — and requiring both simultaneously excludes genuinely over-collateralized firms, so the union of the two conditions identifies the full population whose balance-sheet value the market ignores.
evaluated.reasoning: Every combination in the archive has been an intersection or a rank average, and generation 4 showed intersections truncate the alpha tail while rank averages dilute it; a union has never been tried and is the only combination rule that can *enlarge* the qualifying set, which should broaden and stabilise the long leg rather than narrow it. The two collateral definitions are economically distinct — trade-cycle assets net of every claim versus cash net of enforceable debt — and the archive shows each carries independent alpha (5.9% and 3.9%), so the union tests whether they identify overlapping or complementary firms. Coverage should equal the better-covered of the two legs, near 0.14.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap on Sales With Eroding Earned Capital
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(re, at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high sales-to-price multiple signals a trap when accumulated earned capital has been eroding year after year, because the firm is converting shareholder equity into operating losses at a steady rate that the low multiple is correctly anticipating.
evaluated.reasoning: The distress leg is a five-year trend in retained earnings intensity, which is not a monotone relative of leverage — a low-debt firm can be steadily burning earned capital while a high-debt firm can be rebuilding it — so this avoids the algebraic collapse into liabilities-over-assets that the critic identified. It also tests deterioration rate rather than a distress level, a distinction the archive's short-side signals have never made, and pairs it with the revenue multiple that has produced the strongest cross-sectional slopes in this search. The five-year trend costs coverage comparable to other temporal archive signals, around 0.11.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Depth Plus Claim Coverage by Earnings
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(pi, lt))
evaluated.hypothesis: Asset-backed cheapness and the ability to service outstanding claims out of current earnings are the two independent guarantees a cheap equity can offer; the firms that provide both are the compensated value cases, and those providing neither are the distressed traps whose price is a forecast.
evaluated.reasoning: Pretax income scaled by total liabilities is a debt-service capacity measure rather than a profitability measure, and it appeared in the archive only alongside the alpha-free claims-per-liquid-asset leg, so its pairing with the alpha-carrying discount has never been observed. The leg is smooth and roughly symmetric across the cross-section, the property that converted the generation-8 composite into the archive's only jointly strong signal, while remaining a distress variable rather than a second valuation ratio. Comparing its outcome with Signal 1 identifies whether the missing slope is best supplied by a second valuation anchor or by a solvency-flow channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Discounted Collateral Being Distributed
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A liquid cushion only becomes shareholder value when it is paid out; a firm trading below its net liquid assets while returning cash to shareholders is demonstrating both that the collateral is real and that management intends to deliver it, whereas a hoarded cushion can be consumed indefinitely.
evaluated.reasoning: Distribution policy is the one mechanism in this theme that has never been evaluated — every conditioner tested has described the balance sheet or its rate of change, none the channel through which a discount actually closes — and it directly addresses the standing objection that net-net alphas come from firms that simply sit on idle assets. The zero-dividend mass places non-payers at the bottom of the second leg, so the long leg is a well-defined set of discounted payers, which is the population the hypothesis names; the interpretation does not depend on the composition of the short leg. Coverage should remain near 0.12 since dividends are reported for the full universe including zeros.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Depth Plus Near-Term Liquidity Coverage
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(act, lct))
evaluated.hypothesis: Total-claim coverage and near-term claim coverage are different guarantees: a firm can have liquid assets exceeding all liabilities yet still face a maturity mismatch if most of those claims fall due within the year, and only the firm that is safe on both timescales offers cheapness free of distress.
evaluated.reasoning: The second leg carries no price term at all, which removes the mechanical inverse-price collinearity the critic identified in pairing two market-cap-deflated value ratios, so any joint improvement must come from the timing dimension rather than from stacking two forms of the same cheapness. The current ratio is bounded, smooth and near-universally reported, the profile that converted the generation-8 additive construction into the archive's only jointly strong signal, and it measures a distress state the cushion level cannot express. Coverage should be full.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Free Liquid Assets After Claims and Price
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), act), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: For each dollar of liquid assets a firm holds, some part is owed to creditors, some part is already paid for by the equity market, and the remainder is free value handed to the buyer; the size of that free remainder per dollar of liquid assets is the cleanest single statement of collateral-backed mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the weighted kitchen-sink rank blend with one interpretable ratio that is not a monotone transform of any archive signal: deflating the dollar discount by total assets destroyed the alpha (−1.9%) while deflating by market value produced the tail-only champion, and gross current assets is the intermediate deflator that keeps the market price inside the numerator where it belongs while bounding the measure from above. Because the denominator is a positive, slowly varying scale variable, the resulting regressor is smooth across the whole cross-section rather than concentrated in a skewed tail, which is exactly the property associated with usable Fama-MacBeth slopes in this archive. It combines the discount, the claims, and the price in a single economic quantity rather than averaging three ranked proxies with implicit unequal weights.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cushion Depth Plus Distant Debt Maturities
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What converts a discounted balance sheet into a restructuring is a maturity that must be refinanced now; a firm whose claims are mostly long-dated can wait for the discount to close, while one facing an imminent maturity wall must transact at distressed prices regardless of how much collateral it holds.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not the creditor-identity variable already evaluated: debt-in-current-liabilities as a share of total claims measures *when* obligations come due, whereas the tested gate measured what fraction of claims are financial rather than trade, and two firms with identical debt mixes can have opposite maturity profiles. Timing of claims is the last untested dimension of the creditor side in this archive and is economically the trigger mechanism for forced liquidation. Scaling by total liabilities rather than by debt keeps the ratio defined for debt-free firms, avoiding the zero-denominator coverage loss that a debt-maturity share would create.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Expensive Collateral With Eroding Earned Capital
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act), NEG(TREND(RATIO(re, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The genuine trap is not a cheap levered firm but one where all claims — market equity plus creditor claims — are priced expensively against the liquid assets backing them while accumulated earned capital erodes year after year, so the claim structure is overvalued relative to shrinking substance.
evaluated.reasoning: The valuation leg is deliberately oriented toward expensiveness rather than leverage, which repairs the sign inconsistency the critic identified: the archive shows the negated form of this exact ratio produced an FMB slope of +4.17, so the un-negated form should deliver a reliably negative slope aligned with the negative expected sign, unlike every liabilities-to-market-value construction tried so far. Pairing it additively with the multi-year erosion of earned capital keeps both legs smooth and continuous, so the bottom of the score is a differentiated population rather than the undifferentiated mixture that MIN gates produced on the short side. This is the archive's best remaining chance at a short-side signal with both metrics pointing the same way.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Value Gated by Going-Concern Flags
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), ADD(INDICATOR(re, 0), INDICATOR(SUB(act, lct), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: The value premium is conditional: it accrues to cheap firms with positive retained earnings and positive working capital, while cheap firms failing both going-concern screens have valuations that reflect genuine default risk and earn no premium.
considered.reasoning: The indicator sum acts as a 0/1/2 multiplier that switches the value exposure off for firms with a deficit in accumulated earnings and a liquidity shortfall, so extreme cheapness among distressed firms is collapsed to the bottom of the cross-section. This is an explicitly conditional interaction rather than an additive blend of two effects. Winsorizing book-to-market prevents a handful of near-zero-market-cap firms from dominating the long leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheapness Times Deleveraging
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What separates value opportunities from traps is the direction of the distress state: cheap firms actively reducing their liability burden are recovering and repricing upward, while equally cheap firms whose leverage is rising are sliding toward distress.
considered.reasoning: The cheapness rank sets the magnitude of the bet and the year-over-year change in the liabilities-to-assets ratio sets its direction, so the signal goes long cheap deleveraging firms and short cheap re-levering firms. This uses a change-in-distress state rather than a level screen, capturing information that static leverage filters miss. Winsorizing the leverage change limits distortion from restructurings and large acquisitions.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap Chronic Loss Trap
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(ib), 0), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Deep cheapness accompanied by repeated annual losses identifies lottery-like distressed equities whose low price reflects a persistent inability to generate earnings; these firms underperform despite apparently attractive multiples.
considered.reasoning: Counting loss years over five fiscal years measures the persistence, not just the presence, of financial trouble, and multiplying by the cheapness rank isolates the specific cell of the value/distress grid where the trap story applies. considered.name: Weakest-Link Value Solvency Score
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)))))

considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cash Yield Net of Near-Term Debt Maturities
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dlc), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)

considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Net-Leverage-Adjusted Residual Cheapness
considered.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at)))

considered.name: Cheap Non-Taxpayer
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(txt, at), 3))))

considered.name: Cheap at Own Liquidity Trough
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(wcap, at), 5))))

considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, lt))))

considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), at), 1)

considered.name: Dual-Deflated Liquid Claim Coverage
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ceq))

SUMRANK reorders the extreme tail — a firm with a huge discount but a book value composed of illiquid assets no longer dominates — which is a substantive change in portfolio composition, not a rescaling. If both metrics improve jointly, the combined construct becomes the consolidation candidate for later generations.

considered.name: Liquidation Discount With Stable Cushion
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at), 1)))

Comparing this signal's results with the oancf version isolates whether the sustainability condition needs a genuine cash-flow statement or can be inferred from the change in the cushion. The MIN keeps the top region restricted to firms that are both deeply discounted and not depleting.

considered.name: Liquid Cushion per Dollar of Total Claims
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: Scaling the liquid cushion by the total market value of all claims — equity plus creditor claims — measures how much of the entire capital structure is already covered by liquid assets, distinguishing genuinely over-collateralized firms from small-equity firms whose discount is an artifact of a collapsed share price sitting on top of heavy debt.

considered.name: Fixed-Charge Burden Behind a Cheap Multiple
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(ebitda, pi), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The wedge between EBITDA and pretax income is the firm's annual fixed charge — interest plus depreciation — so a cheap cash-earnings multiple sitting on top of a large fixed-charge load means the operating cash is committed before shareholders see it, making the cheapness a distress discount rather than an opportunity.

Because both legs are continuously distributed across nearly all firms, the top region is a clean high-yield, high-burden cell with no tie blocks. Its expected negative sign also gives the batch a short-side test to complement the four long-side liquidation constructs.

considered.name: Revenue Cheapness With Solvent Liquidity
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at)))
considered.hypothesis: The healthy-cheap versus trap distinction should not be specific to balance-sheet valuation: a firm cheap on revenue is a compensated value case when its current assets already exceed all liabilities, and a distressed one when creditors have first claim on the entire asset base.

Deflating the cushion by assets here is deliberate — the price dimension already enters through the sales multiple, so the two legs stay economically independent. Sales are reported nearly universally, so coverage should match the archive's best signals.

considered.name: Worst-Case Liquid Cushion to Price
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(TS_MIN(SUB(act, lt), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The collateral that protects a cheap stock is not the cushion reported at one convenient date but the minimum net liquid position the firm has actually sustained over recent years; measuring the discount against that demonstrated floor separates durably over-collateralized firms from those whose current-year cushion was manufactured by an asset sale, a debt drawdown, or a working-capital build.

It is economically distinct from the archive winner because it reorders firms by the reliability of their creditor-adjusted liquid backing rather than by its latest level, which is exactly the healthy-versus-illusory-cheapness distinction and should stabilize portfolio composition and raise ls_talpha. The three-year window is short enough to keep coverage close to the archive's 0.12 while still requiring the cushion to have survived a full reporting cycle.

considered.name: Worst-Case Cushion With Profitable Operations
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(TS_MIN(SUB(act, lt), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(pi, at)))
considered.hypothesis: A deep discount to a durable liquid cushion is compensated mispricing when the operating business is still profitable, and a rational forecast of cash burn when it is not; the profitable subset of deeply discounted firms should carry the entire abnormal return.

considered.name: Own-History Cheapness With Solvent Balance Sheet
considered.expression: MIN(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm trading at the cheapest valuation of its own five-year history is either being repriced for newly revealed distress or is temporarily out of favor; the solvency of its balance sheet decides which, so time-series cheapness conditioned on liquid solvency should isolate genuine mispricing.
considered.reasoning: All archive valuation legs are cross-sectional, which conflates permanently cheap business models with firms that have actually de-rated; a within-firm valuation percentile removes that fixed effect and asks a different economic question. Combining it with an asset-scaled solvency leg keeps the price dimension in only one leg, so the two components remain economically independent. The five-year window costs some coverage, as it did for the archive's liquidity-trough signal (0.111), which is an acceptable price for testing a genuinely new valuation anchor.

considered.name: Unimpairable Cash Cushion to Price
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(che, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: In genuine distress, receivables are not collected and inventory sells at a fraction of carrying value, so only cash survives the state of the world that matters; a firm whose cash alone exceeds every liability and still trades at a discount holds collateral that cannot be impaired.
considered.reasoning: The archive has repeatedly varied which *liabilities* are netted but never isolated which *assets* do the work with full coverage — the one cash-based attempt bundled in operating cash flow and lost a third of the sample. considered.name: Cushion Discount Without Dilution
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Management's financing behavior reveals which kind of cheap firm it is running: a firm sitting on a liquid cushion that keeps issuing shares is funding losses and diluting the very claim that looks cheap, whereas one whose share count is flat or shrinking is letting existing holders keep the discount.

considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))

considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), ABS(TS_MIN(pi, 5)))))

considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), SUB(revt, pi))))

considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(pi, at), 5)))
