considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Levered Diluter Death Spiral
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(GROWTH(csho, 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose liabilities dwarf its market value and which is simultaneously issuing shares is funding creditor obligations by diluting equity holders at depressed prices, a self-reinforcing transfer from shareholders to creditors that predicts continued underperformance.
considered.reasoning: This isolates the financing behavior that turns market-value leverage into realized equity loss, a mechanism the archive has approached only from the asset side and never tested on the short side. Both legs are continuously distributed with no tie blocks among the levered universe, and the pairing is economically tight: neither high market leverage alone nor issuance alone identifies the transfer, but their intersection does. A reliable negative alpha here would give the search a genuine short-leg mechanism to pair with the cushion long leg in the final consolidation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Productive Cushion at a Discount
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(revt, act)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms trading below net liquid asset value split into two economically opposite groups — working businesses whose inventory and receivables are turning over to generate sales, and dormant shells whose current assets sit idle while overhead consumes them — and only the productive group's discount closes.
considered.reasoning: This introduces asset productivity, a channel the archive has never tested, in place of recombining two collinear cushion constructs: revenue per dollar of current assets says whether the collateral is a live operating base or a stagnant pile, which is the sharpest available distinction between compensated cheapness and a slow-burning trap. Because the second leg shares the current-asset base with the first, it should refine the deep-discount decile rather than displace it — the failure mode the no-dilution intersection exposed. Both inputs are universally reported, so coverage should hold near the archive's 0.12.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Discount Plus Per-Share Cushion Accretion
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), GROWTH(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), csho), 1))
considered.hypothesis: What protects the holder of a cheap asset-backed equity is not the share count and not the total cushion separately, but whether net liquid assets *per share* are rising; a firm accreting liquid value per share is compounding the discount in the owner's favor, while one whose per-share cushion is shrinking is either burning assets or issuing stock against them.
considered.reasoning: This is not the earlier operator swap: the second leg is a new quantity that fuses the asset-accumulation and dilution channels the archive tested separately, resolving why the no-dilution filter helped the cross-sectional slope but destroyed the tail — issuance only matters when it outpaces cushion growth. The additive combination keeps deeply discounted firms at the top of the score while the accretion leg, which is continuous and roughly symmetric, orders the middle of the distribution and should lift the FMB slope. Coverage costs only one year of history, keeping the sample close to the archive's best signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap Book Value in Asset-Heavy Firms
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), revt)))
considered.hypothesis: If the effect is really about balance-sheet dominance rather than about the specific net-net threshold, then ordinary book-to-market conditioned on a large liquid cushion per dollar of revenue should reproduce it; if instead the price-below-liquid-assets condition is essential, this variant will be much weaker.
considered.reasoning: This is the decisive ablation the archive still lacks: every strong result has used net liquid assets in the numerator over price, so we cannot yet tell whether the alpha requires that specific comparison or only requires cheapness plus an operations-light liquid balance sheet. Book-to-market has repeatedly produced strong FMB slopes (3.5–4.0) with weak or negative alphas in this archive, so pairing it with the newly identified conditioner tests directly whether that conditioner is what converts a factor-explained value tilt into abnormal return. Coverage matches the archive's best signals since all inputs are standard.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Discount With Uninflated Working Capital
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(SUB(GROWTH(act, 1), GROWTH(revt, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: A liquid cushion is only worth its carrying value if it is turning over; when current assets grow far faster than sales, the balance sheet is accumulating unsellable inventory and uncollectible receivables, so the apparent liquidation floor is overstated and the cheapness is a genuine distress signal.
considered.reasoning: Every archive test of cushion quality has varied which claims are netted or how large the cushion is; none has questioned whether the reported current assets are realizable, which is exactly the accounting failure that turns a net-net into a trap. The leg is a difference of two growth rates, so it is continuously distributed and roughly symmetric — the property that lifted the FMB slope in the two-sided score — while remaining economically tied to the cushion rather than orthogonal to it. This is the batch's most direct attempt to raise the cross-sectional slope without truncating the alpha-bearing tail.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt-Free Cash Earnings Yield
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), act))))
considered.hypothesis: On the earnings side of valuation, cheapness is compensated when no enforceable debt stands between the operating cash flow and the shareholder; a high cash-earnings yield with interest-bearing debt small relative to liquid assets is the going-concern analogue of a net-net.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested the earnings channel almost exclusively on the trap side — high yield with high leverage or high fixed charges, both around −4% alpha — so the symmetric positive case has never been evaluated, leaving the theme's central claim only half tested. Scaling debt by current assets rather than total assets measures whether the enforceable claims could be extinguished immediately, which is the distress-relevant comparison and mirrors the construct that scored best in generation 5 (5.6% alpha, t=4.11). Both legs are broadly reported, so coverage should stay near 0.14.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Discount With Non-Expanding Claims
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(lt, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A liquid cushion priced at a discount is safe only if creditors are not expanding their claim on it; rising total liabilities mean the firm is funding operations by borrowing against the very assets that constitute the margin of safety.
considered.reasoning: The archive has conditioned the cushion on its own change and on share issuance but never on the growth of the claims that are netted out of it, even though liability expansion is the mechanism by which a net-net silently becomes a levered shell. The leg is cushion-related through lt, so it should refine rather than displace the top decile — the distinction generation 4 established between correlated and orthogonal conditioners. It also gives a clean contrast with Signal 3: asset-side inflation versus liability-side expansion as competing explanations for why a cushion fails to protect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Negative Implied Price of Operations
considered.expression: WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(MUL(prcc_f, csho), SUB(act, lt)), revt)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: Market capitalization decomposes into the net liquid cushion plus whatever the market is paying for the operating business; when that residual stub price is deeply negative relative to the revenue the business actually produces, investors are being handed the operations for free because they extrapolate current operating disappointment.
considered.reasoning: Rather than re-scaling the cushion by another operating denominator — the collinearity the critic identified — this construct isolates the *residual* the archive has never measured: price minus cushion, which is the market's standalone valuation of the going concern, benchmarked against the revenue that concern generates. It states the theme's core question directly, because a negative stub price means the valuation reflects operating distress while the distress-relevant collateral is intact and unpriced. Revenue is strictly positive for the operating universe, so the deflator does not sign-flip, and the measure is continuous across the whole cross-section rather than being a tail indicator.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Claims Outgrowing the Business Behind Them
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUB(GROWTH(lt, 1), GROWTH(revt, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A levered firm becomes a trap when its creditor claims expand faster than the revenue base that must service them; the equity of such a firm is a shrinking residual on a widening obligation, and its low valuation is a forecast rather than a discount.
considered.reasoning: The second leg is a new quantity for this archive — the divergence between liability growth and revenue growth — rather than a merger of the previously tested volatility and issuance gates, and it captures deterioration in debt-servicing capacity that no static leverage ratio or second-moment measure can express. Pairing it with market-value leverage is what makes the claim cross-theme: the same liability expansion is benign for a firm whose equity is richly valued and lethal for one whose market value is already a stub. Both legs are continuously distributed with no tie blocks, and only one year of history is required, so coverage should remain near 0.13.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cushion Backing Minus Claim Escalation
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(SUB(GROWTH(lt, 1), GROWTH(revt, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The two ends of this theme are distinct populations: over-collateralized cheap firms earn a premium, and firms whose creditor claims are growing faster than the revenue that must service them underperform, so a single score should rank the first group at the top and the second at the bottom.
considered.reasoning: The claim-escalation leg produced the archive's cleanest short-side result (−4.1% alpha, t=−3.54) but, used as a MIN gate, growth legs have consistently destroyed the long tail; combining additively lets each leg populate its own extreme without the intersection truncating either. This is the only construction in the archive that puts a genuinely different economic population in each leg rather than filtering one population twice. If it delivers a mid-single-digit alpha with a materially positive slope, it resolves the archive's central tension by construction rather than by transformation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Chronic Net-Net Status Count
considered.expression: TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 0), 5)
considered.hypothesis: A single year of market capitalization below net liquid asset value can be a stale price or a transient dislocation, but a firm that has satisfied this condition in most of the last five years is persistently and knowably over-collateralized, and the market's continued refusal to price the collateral is the mispricing.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the deflator recombination with a genuinely different construction — a discrete count of how many annual observations satisfied the balance-sheet-versus-price condition, rather than another continuous ratio whose slope the archive has repeatedly shown to be near zero. A five-level integer regressor is exactly the kind of well-conditioned variable that can produce a meaningful Fama-MacBeth slope, and it selects the top portfolio on persistence rather than on the magnitude of a skewed ratio, so the portfolios differ substantively from every archive signal. The trade-off is a large tie block at zero, which the coverage and Sharpe diagnostics will reveal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Own-History Extreme Asset Discount
considered.expression: TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5)
considered.hypothesis: Firms differ permanently in how much liquid collateral their business model carries, so what identifies mispricing is not the level of the asset discount but whether a firm now sits at the widest discount of its own recent history — the point at which the market has repriced the equity without any corresponding change in the collateral.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the flagged price-drawdown leg, the valuation anchor here is not the price path but the price relative to a contemporaneous balance-sheet quantity, so it is not a restatement of nearness-to-high or long-horizon reversal; a firm can reach its own extreme through a falling price or a growing cushion, and both are informative about the same wedge. Within-firm ranking removes the permanent industry and business-model component that makes the cross-sectional level so lumpy and tail-concentrated, which is the archive's diagnosed cause of near-zero slopes. Coverage should land near 0.11, consistent with other five-year constructs in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Levered Firm Liquidating Its Current Assets
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(act, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: When a firm whose liabilities already dwarf its market value is shrinking its current assets, it is meeting obligations by consuming inventory and collecting receivables without replacing them — an orderly self-liquidation in which the equity holder is last in line and receives nothing.
considered.reasoning: This drops the contested price-path leg entirely and pairs market-value leverage with a purely accounting measure of balance-sheet contraction, a channel the archive has never tested on the short side and one that is economically distinct from liability growth, share issuance, and earnings volatility. The two legs share no variable, so the top region isolates precisely the levered-and-contracting cell the hypothesis names, and the interpretation does not depend on the composition of the bottom region. Both inputs are universally reported, so coverage should hold near 0.13 with only one year of history required.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Claims Value per Dollar of Liquid Assets
considered.expression: NEG(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Every claim on a firm — equity at market value and liabilities at face value — is ultimately a claim on its assets, so the price the market places on each dollar of liquid current assets is the cleanest statement of asset-backed cheapness; paying little for each such dollar is compensated, paying much is not.
considered.reasoning: This is not a monotone transform of the total-claims cushion signal: that measure is (act−lt)/(ME+lt), a function of two independent ratios, whereas this is (ME+lt)/act, which orders firms differently whenever leverage and market valuation move apart. Because the denominator is gross current assets, the quantity is strictly positive and bounded away from the explosive skew that has kept the archive's FMB slopes near zero, giving a plausible path to joint strength rather than tail-only alpha. It also treats creditors and shareholders symmetrically, which is the correct economics when asking what the market pays for liquid collateral.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap Liquid Assets With Covered Claims
considered.expression: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act)), RATIO(pi, lt))
considered.hypothesis: Healthy cheapness combines a low price per dollar of liquid assets with pretax earnings large enough to service the outstanding claims; the trap is the opposite corner, where claims are expensive relative to liquid assets and earnings cannot cover them.
considered.reasoning: This is not an operator swap on an existing pair: both legs are new to the archive — the price paid per dollar of liquid assets and pretax income scaled by total claims rather than by assets, which measures debt-service capacity rather than profitability. Because the two legs use different accounting anchors and neither is a monotone function of the other, the additive score populates its extremes with economically different firms, giving genuinely new portfolio evidence rather than a smoothed version of a tested spread. Both components are continuously distributed across essentially the whole universe, which is the property most likely to convert the archive's tail-only alpha into a signal with a coherent cross-sectional slope.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cushion Discount With Cash-Heavy Collateral
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(che, act)))
considered.hypothesis: Two firms with identical net liquid cushions differ in how much of that cushion is cash rather than inventory and receivables; the cash-heavy one can actually deliver the collateral to shareholders, while the inventory-heavy one holds assets whose realizable value falls precisely when the firm needs it.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested cash *instead of* working capital — the cash-only cushion delivered a weaker 3.9% alpha with a negative Sharpe — but never cash as a *composition* condition on the full cushion, which is a different economic claim about realizability rather than about which assets to count. The gate is a ratio of components of the same current-asset base, so it should refine the deep-discount decile rather than replace it with an orthogonal population. Interpreted alongside Signal 4, it separates the two ways a cushion can fail: unrealizable assets versus inflexible creditors.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cushion Discount With Flexible Creditors
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt))))
considered.hypothesis: What matters for a discounted firm is not how large its liabilities are but who holds them: trade payables and accruals can be renegotiated or stretched in a downturn, whereas bondholders and banks can accelerate, so a cushion standing behind mostly non-financial claims is far safer at the same leverage.
considered.reasoning: Every leverage-related conditioner in the archive has measured the *magnitude* of claims — debt over assets, debt over current assets, liability growth — and none has measured their *composition*, even though creditor type determines whether distress becomes a forced event. Scaling debt by total liabilities rather than by an asset base makes this a pure mix variable, uncorrelated with firm size and only mildly correlated with the leverage levels already tested. Contrasting its result with Signal 2, which uses the same debt items scaled by current assets, identifies whether coverage or creditor identity is the operative mechanism.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cushion Depth Plus Cheap Liquid Assets
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act)))
considered.hypothesis: The depth of the net-of-claims discount and the price paid per gross dollar of liquid assets are two distinct statements about the same balance sheet — the first is extreme and tail-concentrated, the second smooth and pervasive — and a firm ranked highly on both is cheap in a way that neither measure alone establishes.
considered.reasoning: This is the last disciplined attempt to close the archive's central gap: the first leg carries essentially all of the documented alpha (5.9%, t=4.48) but a slope of 0.48, while the second leg carries a 4.17 slope and Sharpe 0.411 with almost no alpha, and the two are related but not monotone transforms of one another since one nets liabilities out of the numerator and the other adds them to it. Additive combination keeps deeply discounted firms near the top instead of intersecting them away, so a mid-to-high single-digit alpha with a slope above 2 is a realistic outcome rather than a smoothing artifact. If it succeeds it becomes the final recommended signal; if it fails, the evidence will have shown the alpha and the slope to be genuinely irreconcilable in this family.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Stress-Tested Cushion to Price
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), ABS(TS_MIN(DELTA(SUB(act, lt), 1), 5))), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The collateral that should support a cheap equity is not today's net liquid position but what would remain after a repeat of the worst single-year erosion the firm has actually experienced; a discount to that stress-tested residual is a discount to collateral the firm has demonstrated it can retain under duress.
considered.reasoning: This is not a lookback-window tweak: the history is used to estimate a firm-specific shock magnitude — the largest annual decline in net current assets — which is then subtracted from the current cushion, producing a value-at-risk style collateral measure that no archive signal computes. It targets the failure mode the whole family faces, namely cushions that evaporate between reporting dates, and because it remains a single continuous ratio it cannot truncate the alpha-bearing decile the way conditioning gates repeatedly have. Firms with volatile working capital are demoted even when their current cushion looks large, so the portfolio composition differs materially from the archived three-year-minimum version.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Either-Form Collateral Discount
considered.expression: MAX(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms hold unpriced collateral in different forms — some as working capital in excess of all claims, others as cash in excess of interest-bearing debt — and requiring both simultaneously excludes genuinely over-collateralized firms, so the union of the two conditions identifies the full population whose balance-sheet value the market ignores.
considered.reasoning: Every combination in the archive has been an intersection or a rank average, and generation 4 showed intersections truncate the alpha tail while rank averages dilute it; a union has never been tried and is the only combination rule that can *enlarge* the qualifying set, which should broaden and stabilise the long leg rather than narrow it. The two collateral definitions are economically distinct — trade-cycle assets net of every claim versus cash net of enforceable debt — and the archive shows each carries independent alpha (5.9% and 3.9%), so the union tests whether they identify overlapping or complementary firms. Coverage should equal the better-covered of the two legs, near 0.14.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cheap on Sales With Eroding Earned Capital
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(re, at), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: A high sales-to-price multiple signals a trap when accumulated earned capital has been eroding year after year, because the firm is converting shareholder equity into operating losses at a steady rate that the low multiple is correctly anticipating.
considered.reasoning: The distress leg is a five-year trend in retained earnings intensity, which is not a monotone relative of leverage — a low-debt firm can be steadily burning earned capital while a high-debt firm can be rebuilding it — so this avoids the algebraic collapse into liabilities-over-assets that the critic identified. It also tests deterioration rate rather than a distress level, a distinction the archive's short-side signals have never made, and pairs it with the revenue multiple that has produced the strongest cross-sectional slopes in this search. The five-year trend costs coverage comparable to other temporal archive signals, around 0.11.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cushion Depth Plus Claim Coverage by Earnings
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(pi, lt))
considered.hypothesis: Asset-backed cheapness and the ability to service outstanding claims out of current earnings are the two independent guarantees a cheap equity can offer; the firms that provide both are the compensated value cases, and those providing neither are the distressed traps whose price is a forecast.
considered.reasoning: Pretax income scaled by total liabilities is a debt-service capacity measure rather than a profitability measure, and it appeared in the archive only alongside the alpha-free claims-per-liquid-asset leg, so its pairing with the alpha-carrying discount has never been observed. The leg is smooth and roughly symmetric across the cross-section, the property that converted the generation-8 composite into the archive's only jointly strong signal, while remaining a distress variable rather than a second valuation ratio. Comparing its outcome with Signal 1 identifies whether the missing slope is best supplied by a second valuation anchor or by a solvency-flow channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Discounted Collateral Being Distributed
considered.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: A liquid cushion only becomes shareholder value when it is paid out; a firm trading below its net liquid assets while returning cash to shareholders is demonstrating both that the collateral is real and that management intends to deliver it, whereas a hoarded cushion can be consumed indefinitely.
considered.reasoning: Distribution policy is the one mechanism in this theme that has never been evaluated — every conditioner tested has described the balance sheet or its rate of change, none the channel through which a discount actually closes — and it directly addresses the standing objection that net-net alphas come from firms that simply sit on idle assets. The zero-dividend mass places non-payers at the bottom of the second leg, so the long leg is a well-defined set of discounted payers, which is the population the hypothesis names; the interpretation does not depend on the composition of the short leg. Coverage should remain near 0.12 since dividends are reported for the full universe including zeros.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cushion Depth Plus Near-Term Liquidity Coverage
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(act, lct))
considered.hypothesis: Total-claim coverage and near-term claim coverage are different guarantees: a firm can have liquid assets exceeding all liabilities yet still face a maturity mismatch if most of those claims fall due within the year, and only the firm that is safe on both timescales offers cheapness free of distress.
considered.reasoning: The second leg carries no price term at all, which removes the mechanical inverse-price collinearity the critic identified in pairing two market-cap-deflated value ratios, so any joint improvement must come from the timing dimension rather than from stacking two forms of the same cheapness. The current ratio is bounded, smooth and near-universally reported, the profile that converted the generation-8 additive construction into the archive's only jointly strong signal, and it measures a distress state the cushion level cannot express. Coverage should be full.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Free Liquid Assets After Claims and Price
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), act), 1)
considered.hypothesis: For each dollar of liquid assets a firm holds, some part is owed to creditors, some part is already paid for by the equity market, and the remainder is free value handed to the buyer; the size of that free remainder per dollar of liquid assets is the cleanest single statement of collateral-backed mispricing.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the weighted kitchen-sink rank blend with one interpretable ratio that is not a monotone transform of any archive signal: deflating the dollar discount by total assets destroyed the alpha (−1.9%) while deflating by market value produced the tail-only champion, and gross current assets is the intermediate deflator that keeps the market price inside the numerator where it belongs while bounding the measure from above. Because the denominator is a positive, slowly varying scale variable, the resulting regressor is smooth across the whole cross-section rather than concentrated in a skewed tail, which is exactly the property associated with usable Fama-MacBeth slopes in this archive. It combines the discount, the claims, and the price in a single economic quantity rather than averaging three ranked proxies with implicit unequal weights.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cushion Depth Plus Distant Debt Maturities
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: What converts a discounted balance sheet into a restructuring is a maturity that must be refinanced now; a firm whose claims are mostly long-dated can wait for the discount to close, while one facing an imminent maturity wall must transact at distressed prices regardless of how much collateral it holds.
considered.reasoning: This is not the creditor-identity variable already evaluated: debt-in-current-liabilities as a share of total claims measures *when* obligations come due, whereas the tested gate measured what fraction of claims are financial rather than trade, and two firms with identical debt mixes can have opposite maturity profiles. Timing of claims is the last untested dimension of the creditor side in this archive and is economically the trigger mechanism for forced liquidation. Scaling by total liabilities rather than by debt keeps the ratio defined for debt-free firms, avoiding the zero-denominator coverage loss that a debt-maturity share would create.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Expensive Collateral With Eroding Earned Capital
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt), act), NEG(TREND(RATIO(re, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: The genuine trap is not a cheap levered firm but one where all claims — market equity plus creditor claims — are priced expensively against the liquid assets backing them while accumulated earned capital erodes year after year, so the claim structure is overvalued relative to shrinking substance.
considered.reasoning: The valuation leg is deliberately oriented toward expensiveness rather than leverage, which repairs the sign inconsistency the critic identified: the archive shows the negated form of this exact ratio produced an FMB slope of +4.17, so the un-negated form should deliver a reliably negative slope aligned with the negative expected sign, unlike every liabilities-to-market-value construction tried so far. Pairing it additively with the multi-year erosion of earned capital keeps both legs smooth and continuous, so the bottom of the score is a differentiated population rather than the undifferentiated mixture that MIN gates produced on the short side. This is the archive's best remaining chance at a short-side signal with both metrics pointing the same way.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: SUMRANK is an additive, fully compensatory blend, so the stated claim that "a firm scores high only if it is simultaneously cheap and financially resilient" is false — a very cheap firm with terrible solvency still ranks high — and the construct is in any case a well-trodden value-plus-quality (retained-earnings / cash-coverage) composite.

The 0/1/2 multiplier is a genuinely conditional switch and the expression matches the hypothesis, but it is close in spirit to Piotroski-style value screening and the short leg becomes an undifferentiated mass of zero-flag firms regardless of valuation, so the alpha may be driven by a plain distress short rather than by conditioning the value premium.

This is EBITDA/EV, a directly published and heavily replicated value anomaly (Loughran–Wellman, Gray–Vogel), not a cross-theme discovery, and the unguarded denominator can approach zero or turn negative for highly cash-rich firms, producing sign-flipped extremes.

A bare product of two z-scores is sign-symmetric, so the long leg pools cheap net-cash firms with *expensive net-debt* firms — exactly the quadrant the hypothesis calls most distressed — which the reasoning silently omits and which contradicts the expected sign.

The magnitude-times-direction construction is internally consistent and change-in-leverage conditioning on value is a defensible cross-theme test, though it overlaps the known net-debt-issuance/financing anomaly and its behavior hinges on whether RANK is nonnegative or centered (a centered rank would flip the sign for expensive firms and break the stated logic).

The loss-persistence-times-cheapness cell is a coherent value-trap test with a correctly signed expression, but roughly two-thirds of firms will score exactly zero, so the "long" leg is a large tie block and the resulting spread is essentially a short-only distress bet that may add little beyond the known financial-distress anomaly.

The distress inputs (lt/at and re/at) are precisely the ingredients already tested in the archive's going-concern-flag and weakest-link value/solvency signals, and the multiplicative form leaves the sign ambiguous — RANK(B/M) enters monotonically and earned a *positive* FMB slope in the archive, so a product that is high for all cheap firms is unlikely to deliver the stated negative expected sign.

This is the same RANK(B/M)×RANK(distress) template with act/lct swapped in, and act−lct was already one of the two going-concern screens in the archive's generation-0 signal, so it is a near-rediscovery with the same unresolved sign ambiguity from the dominant value component.

Differencing S/P and pretax-E/P ranks on a common price denominator collapses cross-sectionally into (negative) pretax profit margin, i.e. a repackaging of the well-documented profitability/RMW anomaly rather than a genuine cross-theme mechanism, and negative pi makes the E/P rank ordering economically incoherent in exactly the distressed tail the hypothesis targets.

Persistent near-zero tax expense is a defensible, hard-to-manage going-concern proxy that is genuinely distinct from the leverage, retained-earnings and working-capital channels already in the archive, though the proposal reuses the same value×distress product template and should be checked for whether the negative expected sign survives the mechanically positive B/M component (and for tax-shield/loss-carryforward firms that are cheap but healthy).

Replacing a cross-sectional distress level with a firm-relative TS_RANK of working capital is a substantive design change that separates deterioration from static weakness — a question none of the archive signals can answer — with the main caveats being coverage loss from the five-year history requirement and the need to verify the negative sign is not overwhelmed by the value leg.

critic_notes.target_name: Value Premium Sign Flip on Accumulated Deficit
critic_notes.rationale: SIGN(re) is the same conditioning variable as the archive's INDICATOR(re,0) gate, and since the large majority of firms have re>0 the signal reduces to industry-neutral book-to-market for most of the cross-section — i.e. mostly a restatement of HML with a small sign-flipped tail, making it a variant of an already-evaluated construct rather than a new mechanism.

RANK is a strictly monotone transform of the already-evaluated winsorized `(act-lt)/mktcap`, so the quantile-sorted portfolios — and hence ls_alpha, ls_talpha, ls_sharpe and coverage — are mechanically identical to the archived result, leaving only a re-scaled FMB slope as new information, which makes this a cosmetic rescaling rather than a substantive test (and the underlying quantity is Graham's net-net/NCAV-to-price, a long-published screen).

A genuine one-input contrast against the archive winner that cleanly identifies whether the effect comes from short-term liquidity or total creditor overhang, though working-capital-to-price is itself a familiar Graham-style value screen and the incremental economic novelty is modest.

Adding a flow-sustainability condition to the winning stock-of-liquidity measure is the economically natural next step and the MIN form is internally consistent with the positive expected sign, but the archive already shows MIN-with-oancf constructs delivering weak evidence and the oancf leg will cut coverage, so the prior on incremental gain is only moderate.

Since `ceq ≈ at - lt`, the numerator collapses to roughly non-current assets, making this essentially fixed-plus-intangible-assets-to-price — a standard assets-to-market value proxy that is well documented to predict returns *positively*, directly contradicting the stated negative expected sign.

With roughly half the universe reporting zero dividends, the yield rank is a large tie block and the MIN's bottom region is determined almost entirely by the leverage leg among non-payers, so the long leg becomes "low-leverage non-payers" rather than the clean affordable-payout benchmark the hypothesis describes, confounding the payout-versus-distress interpretation.

critic_notes.target_name: Cash Resources Net of Current Claims to Price
critic_notes.rationale: A coherent, strictly-verifiable-resources refinement of the liquidation-backing construct with a sensible positive denominator, but it mixes a stock (che, lct) with a flow (oancf) without scaling justification and will be highly correlated with both net-cash-to-price and the archive winner, limiting how much independent evidence it can generate.

A three-year moving average of the archive's existing top signal is a cosmetic smoothing variant rather than a new economic mechanism, and it introduces a stale-price contamination (two-year-old market caps in the denominator) that confounds the "persistence" interpretation with slow-moving reversal/momentum effects.

A defensible additivity test of the two archive legs, though it is close to mechanical since (act−lt)/mcap equals (act−lt)/ceq times book-to-market, and the ceq denominator sign-flips for negative-book-equity firms, which will scramble the rank in exactly the distressed tail the signal is meant to separate.

The balance-sheet depletion leg is a genuinely different and coverage-preserving substitute for the oancf filter and the diagnostic comparison is well motivated, but the unwinsorized DELTA leg and the MIN against a near-symmetric change distribution risk letting noisy small changes, rather than discount depth, drive the top decile.

critic_notes.target_name: Liquid Cushion per Dollar of Total Claims
critic_notes.rationale: A clean, well-motivated denominator ablation that isolates whether the effect is equity-price-specific, though placing lt in both numerator and denominator makes the construct partly a leverage measure, so a sign change should not be over-interpreted as evidence about the price channel alone.

critic_notes.target_name: Fixed-Charge Burden Behind a Cheap Multiple
critic_notes.rationale: The channel is distinct from the archive's balance-sheet leverage legs, but EBITDA−PI is dominated by depreciation and special items rather than interest for most firms, so the "cash pledged to creditors" story is likely to be tested as a capital-intensity/accruals effect instead — the label and the mechanism only partly line up.

The best proposal in the batch: it swaps in an independent valuation anchor to test whether liquid solvency conditions the value premium generally or is a book-to-market artifact, with sensible non-overlapping deflators and broad coverage, though sales-to-price is itself a known anomaly with strong industry tilts that should be acknowledged when interpreting the spread.

critic_notes.target_name: Hard-Claims Net Liquid Value to Price
critic_notes.rationale: Internally coherent and cheap to test, but it is a liability-definition tweak that sits mechanically between two already-tested archive constructs ((act−lct)/ME and (act−lt)/ME), so the most likely outcome is an interpolated result with little new economic content beyond the deferred-tax/pension residual.

The expression matches the hypothesis and the substitution of pi/at for oancf/lct is a defensible fix for the coverage truncation that muddied the earlier viability test, though it remains an incremental recombination of two existing archive legs and effectively re-tests the well-known value-plus-profitability intersection.

This is a standard neutralization transform applied directly to the archive's existing best signal, and industry-adjusted valuation ratios are themselves a long-published result (Cohen–Polk, Asness et al.), so it offers a diagnostic at best rather than a new mechanism.

Because both legs share the same numerator, the rank difference is essentially monotone in at/ME, so the signal restates asset-to-market cheapness with a sign opposite to the value premium; it is also the near-negation of the archive's already-tested "Unlevered Versus Levered Cheapness Gap" and a rediscovery of the Penman–Richardson–Tuna leverage component of book-to-price.

critic_notes.target_name: Own-History Cheapness With Solvent Balance Sheet
critic_notes.rationale: The within-firm valuation anchor is genuinely new to this archive and the hypothesis matches the expression, but taking MIN of a coarse 5-observation TS_RANK against a continuous cross-sectional rank will make the signal heavily tie-blocked and often driven by a five-level variable, which risks unstable portfolio composition.

This is a rank-average ensemble of components already tested in the archive, with two highly collinear cushion-to-price legs that will dominate the score, so it adds no new economic hypothesis and its likely metric gains would be attributable to smoothing rather than to any identified mechanism.

This is a near-duplicate of the archive's gen-4 "Loss-Absorption Horizon at a Discount" with only the first leg's cushion swapped for its three-year minimum — two already-tested, highly collinear cushion constructs recombined with the same operator, which is a cosmetic consolidation rather than new economic content.

critic_notes.target_name: Cushion Runway Against Operating Cost Base
critic_notes.rationale: The runway leg (cushion divided by the annual cost base) is a genuinely distinct, continuously distributed alternative to the outlier-driven worst-loss denominator and is internally consistent in sign, though it remains yet another cushion×conditioner MIN in a heavily saturated family and the denominator can flip sign for loss-making high-margin firms.

critic_notes.target_name: Two-Sided Cushion and Earnings Stability Score
critic_notes.rationale: Additively combining asset-backed cheapness with low fundamental-earnings volatility is a coherent response to the documented tail-signal/slope divergence and is sign-consistent, but it edges close to a standard value-plus-quality composite and to the published earnings-volatility anomaly, so the incremental novelty is modest.

Separating enforceable interest-bearing debt from non-triggering trade and accrued claims is the one economically substantive distinction the cushion family has not yet tested, the sign follows naturally from the expression, and coverage should be unimpaired.

This is a pure operator swap (MIN→SUMRANK) on the identical two legs of the archive's gen-4 "Cushion Discount Without Dilution" — precisely the cosmetic variant the objective warns against, and its predicted outcome (alpha between the two parent signals) carries little diagnostic value beyond confirming that MIN truncates tails.

The expression and negative expected sign are internally consistent and it supplies the missing short leg, but the share-issuance effect is a well-known published anomaly and conditioning it on market leverage is a familiar distress-interaction, so it risks being a partial rediscovery rather than a novel cross-theme mechanism.

critic_notes.target_name: Cushion Large Relative to Operating Scale
critic_notes.rationale: The second leg, net liquid assets over revenue, is a near-mechanical duplicate of the already-tested "Cushion Runway Against Operating Cost Base" leg (revt − pi is simply revenue times one minus the margin, so the cross-sectional ranks will be almost perfectly correlated), making this a cosmetic re-specification rather than a new economic conditioner.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheap Book Value in Asset-Heavy Firms
critic_notes.rationale: This is a legitimate and clearly framed ablation of whether the price-below-liquid-assets comparison is essential, but the archive already contains two close cousins (B/M gated by cushion-to-book and revenue-cheapness gated by cushion-to-assets, both with ~zero alpha) that largely pre-answer the question, so its expected informational yield is modest.

Questioning the realizability of the reported current assets via current-asset growth outrunning sales growth is the first genuinely new economic mechanism in this batch and is well matched to the stated hypothesis, though the reviewer should note it partially overlaps the published working-capital-accrual and inventory-growth anomalies and that an unwinsorized growth difference will be rank-dominated by tiny-revenue firms.

Testing the symmetric low-enforceable-debt case on the earnings side is a coherent and untested complement to the two negative-signed earnings-yield gates in the archive, but it is close to the well-documented result that value/earnings-yield strategies work best among low-leverage firms, so novelty is limited and the second leg is identical to the one already used in generation 5.

critic_notes.target_name: Volatile Levered Stub Funding Itself by Dilution
critic_notes.rationale: This is literally the union of two already-evaluated signals — the levered-stub-with-volatile-earnings gate and the levered-diluter gate — with their second legs merged by SUMRANK, which is an ensemble of tested components rather than a substantively new claim, and each ingredient (distress, share issuance, earnings volatility) is an independently published anomaly.

Liability growth is economically distinct from the cushion-change and share-issuance conditioners already tried and provides a clean contrast with the asset-side inflation story, but it is effectively the published net-debt-issuance/external-financing anomaly used as a gate, and the archive pattern shows most such MIN gates merely dilute the base cushion-to-price leg's 5.9% alpha.

critic_notes.target_name: Conservative Cushion per Dollar of Total Claims
critic_notes.rationale: Mechanically sound and sign-consistent, but it is a deflator/numerator recombination of two archive signals whose FMB slopes were both ~0.3, so the stated rationale that adding liabilities to the denominator will "lift the slope" is directly contradicted by the total-claims parent that already did exactly that and still produced a slope of 0.35.

Signs are internally consistent and the two legs do target economically distinct populations, but the construction re-uses the exact SUMRANK(cushion-to-price, quality leg) template already tested in "Two-Sided Cushion and Earnings Stability Score," so the marginal information is the growth-mismatch leg rather than the design.

critic_notes.target_name: Price Collapse With Intact Balance Sheet
critic_notes.rationale: The valuation leg is a coarse annual-price restatement of the well-documented nearness-to-52-week-high / long-term-reversal anomalies, and the proposal never acknowledges that the two published effects imply opposite signs at different horizons, leaving the expected sign asserted rather than argued.

This is the mirror of the previous proposal with the same known price-anomaly leg, and the MIN operator makes its low end a mixture of "near the high" and "low claim ratio" firms, so the spread does not isolate the claimed contrast and the "controlled experiment" interpretation does not hold.

critic_notes.target_name: Log Solvency Distance Including Market Value
critic_notes.rationale: Algebraically (act+mcap)/(lt+mcap) = 1 + (act−lt)/(lt+mcap), so the log is a strictly monotone transform of the archive's "Liquid Cushion per Dollar of Total Claims" and will reproduce its rank-sorted portfolio results exactly, making the "genuinely different market-augmented solvency distance" claim false and the only possible change a mild FMB outlier effect.

This is a pure operator swap (MIN to SUMRANK) on the identical two legs of an existing archive signal — the textbook cosmetic variant the objective warns against — and the proposal's own argument that it "keeps essentially the same firms at the top" concedes it will not deliver substantively new portfolio evidence.

This is a pure lookback-window tweak of the archived "Worst-Case Liquid Cushion to Price" (TS_MIN 3 → 5) applied to an already heavily mined net-net/NCAV construct, i.e. exactly the cosmetic parameter variant the objective warns against, and the extra history will mainly cost coverage and survivorship-clean firm-years.

Both legs are already in the archive with near-identical performance on the same base construct (3-yr min cushion 6.4%/t=4.76; debt-to-current-assets gate 5.6%/t=4.11), so a MIN intersection of two highly overlapping balance-sheet screens is mechanical consolidation whose result is largely predictable and unlikely to be attributable to a new mechanism.

Conditioning the cushion discount on the *composition* of current assets (cash share) is an economically distinct realizability claim rather than a redefinition of the cushion, it is genuinely untested in the archive, the expression's direction matches the stated sign, and the failed che−lt variant provides a clean interpretive contrast.

Debt-to-total-liabilities is a scale-free creditor-mix variable that no archived conditioner captures (all prior leverage gates deflate by an asset base and thus measure magnitude), the acceleration-risk mechanism is coherent, and the paired contrast with the debt/act gate makes the outcome interpretable either way.

Since at ≈ ceq + lt, RANK(NEG(ceq/lt)) is very nearly a monotone transform of RANK(lt/at), so this reduces to the archived "Cash Earnings Yield Pledged to Creditors" with revenue swapped for EBITDA in the valuation leg — a substitution variant, not a new interaction, and the claim of "no shared price term" is undercut by the fact that both legs load on a collapsed market cap.

critic_notes.target_name: Cushion Depth Plus Cheap Liquid Assets
critic_notes.rationale: The combination of the alpha-carrying cushion discount with the slope-carrying claims-per-liquid-asset ratio is untested and explicitly motivated by the documented FMB/alpha divergence with a pre-committed falsification, but the two legs are functions of the same three items and highly related, so the most likely outcome is an interpolation between the known results rather than a genuine reconciliation.

Both legs are established standalone value anomalies (Graham net-net and sales-to-price) sharing the same market-cap denominator, so the rank sum is largely a mechanical inverse-price composite whose stated motivation ("pair the channel with the slope to the channel with the alpha") is metric-fitting rather than an economic mechanism.

critic_notes.target_name: Cushion Depth Plus Claim Coverage by Earnings
critic_notes.rationale: The pairing of the alpha-carrying cushion discount with the earnings-coverage flow leg is a genuinely untested and economically coherent combination, though it is close to a leg-substitution on the archive's gen-7 composite and the two valuation legs involved are themselves highly correlated.

This is a kitchen-sink re-assembly of three already-evaluated components whose two valuation legs are near-collinear, and the nested SUMRANK silently imposes 50/25/25 weights rather than the equal three-channel averaging the reasoning claims.

This is a MIN-to-SUMRANK operator swap on the already-evaluated "Cushion Discount With Flexible Creditors" with identical inputs and hypothesis, i.e. a cosmetic variant rather than a substantively different mechanism.

The payout channel is the one economically distinct conditioner in this theme that the archive has never tested and it directly addresses the "idle shell" objection to net-net alphas, with the caveats that dividend yield shares the price denominator with the cushion leg and the zero-dividend mass creates heavy ties.

critic_notes.target_name: Levered Equity With Eroding Earned Capital
critic_notes.rationale: The negative expected sign on a liabilities-to-market-value leg conflicts with the documented Bhandari leverage premium and with the archive's own lt/market-cap signals, all of which produced positive FMB slopes under a negative-sign hypothesis, so the construction is likely sign-inconsistent as well as a near-duplicate of the gen-8 eroding-capital signal.
